lesson.title: For Loops and Accumulators
lesson.objective: Read, predict and write for loops that build up a result.
lesson.approachReason: The accumulator pattern is best learned by predicting what a loop does first and naming the pattern only after the learner has seen the evidence in traces and outputs.

blocks.heading: A for loop walks through a sequence
blocks.body: for n in [3, 5, 2]: sets n to each value in turn — 3, then 5, then 2. The indented body runs once per value, top to bottom, and the same variable n is reused each trip. When the sequence runs out, the loop stops and the first unindented line runs next.
blocks.example: for letter in "cat": runs the body with letter = "c", then "a", then "t" — three trips, one per character.

blocks.heading: Trace a loop that adds things up
blocks.prompt: Step through the code one line at a time and watch the variables change.
blocks.code:
nums = [4, 1, 6]
total = 0
for n in nums:
    total = total + n
print(total)
blocks.explanation: total is the accumulator. It starts at 0, is updated once per item, and holds 11 when the loop ends.

trace.note: total starts at 0 before the loop.
First trip: n takes the first value.
Second trip: n moves to the next item.
total grows again, keeping the old value.
Third trip: n takes the last item.
The loop is done, so print runs once.

hints: How many items are in the list?
count changes by the same amount on every trip.
blocks.retry: A counter is just an accumulator that adds 1 each trip instead of adding the item.

blocks.heading: The accumulator: one variable that grows across trips
blocks.body: An accumulator is a variable created before the loop, updated inside the loop, and used after the loop ends. Before the loop it holds a starting value — 0 for a sum. Inside, each trip folds one item into it with a line like total = total + n. After the loop, that single variable holds the combined result, which is why you print it outside the body.
blocks.example: For a product you would start at 1, not 0, because multiplying by 0 would wipe out everything on the first trip.

blocks.heading: Worked example: counting the even numbers
blocks.problem: Problem: write a loop that counts how many numbers in [4, 9, 2, 7, 10] are even.

steps.title: Start the counter
steps.why: The variable must exist before the first trip, or there is nothing to add to.

steps.title: Walk through the numbers
steps.why: n takes each value in turn — five trips in total.

steps.title: Test each number
steps.why: % gives the remainder; a remainder of 0 means even. The update only happens on trips where the test passes.

steps.title: Report once
steps.why: Printing inside the body would show a running count each trip; outside shows only the final result.

blocks.answer: Final answer: only 4, 2 and 10 are even, so the loop prints 3.

hints: big only changes on the trips where the test passes.
blocks.retry: Anything that survives to the print line is the sum of the items whose test passed — nothing else.

blocks.heading: Find the bug
blocks.prompt: This loop should add 3 + 6 + 9 and print 18, but it prints 9. One line needs to change.
blocks.code:
nums = [3, 6, 9]
total = 0
for n in nums:
    total = 0
    total = total + n
print(total)
blocks.explanation: Diagnosis rule: if an accumulator never grows past a single item, look for a line inside the loop that resets it.
hints: Read the body line by line: what happens after total is updated?

options.text: Delete the total = 0 inside the loop, keeping the one above it.
options.feedback: Correct. Then each trip adds to what the previous trips built: 3, then 9, then 18.

options.text: Change total = total + n to total = n + total.
options.feedback: Addition order makes no difference here. The reset is what destroys the running total.
That would print 3, 6 and 9 each trip — still no accumulation, and the final value stays wrong.
range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 rather than 3, 6, 9, and the reset inside the loop is untouched.

blocks.heading: Compute the final total
blocks.prompt:
What does this loop print?

total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total = total + n
print(total)

Type the number only.

traps.feedback: 4 is how many numbers the range gives (and also the last value), not their sum.
That is 2 + 3 + 4 — range(1, 5) starts at 1, not 2.
range(1, 5) stops before 5, so 5 is never added.

hints: range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4 — the stop value is excluded.
Add one at a time: 1, then 1 + 2, then ...
text starts as an empty string, so the very first trip writes the first word.
Each trip puts its piece after everything already stored in text.
blocks.retry: Strings accumulate the same way numbers do: start empty, append one piece per trip, print once at the end.

activities.title: What does this loop print?
activities.prompt:
Look at the code below and predict the output before reading anything else.

total = 0
for n in [3, 5, 2]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
activities.reveal: It prints 10. The line total = total + n runs once per item, so total grows: 3, then 8, then 10.

options.feedback: Right — one trip per item, each folding the item into total.
That would need print(n) inside the loop. The print here is outside, so it runs once with the final total.
total starts at 0, but the loop changes it on every trip.
Nothing is wrong with the code — total is defined before it is used, and the indent is correct.

activities.title: Outside the loop or inside the body?
activities.prompt: This loop adds up the numbers in nums. Decide where each line belongs.
activities.reveal: Set up before, update inside, report after — that is the accumulator pattern, and the placement of each line is what makes it work.
buckets: Inside the loop body (runs each trip)

items.bucket: Inside the loop body (runs each trip)

questions.question:
Maya writes:

count = 0
for word in ["hi", "there", "friend", "ok"]:
    count = count + 1
print(count)

What does it print?
questions.explanation: count starts at 0 and increases by 1 on each of the four trips, so the final value is 4.

questions.question:
A shop's sales list is [12, 5, 30, 8]. Sam writes:

big = 0
for s in [12, 5, 30, 8]:
    if s > 10:
        big = big + s
print(big)

What does it print?
questions.explanation: Only 12 and 30 satisfy s > 10, and only those trips add to big, giving 12 + 30 = 42.

questions.question:
Ravi builds a string from words:

text = ""
for w in ["go", "run", "fly"]:
    text = text + w + "!"
print(text)

What is printed?
questions.explanation: text starts empty and each trip appends the current word plus "!", so the pieces pile up in order as go!run!fly!.

trace.blocks: activity > explain > code > check > explain > activity > worked > check > code > problem > check

problems: The module objective includes 'write' for loops that build up a result, but no activity asks the learner to actually compose a loop: prediction, sorting, and multiple-choice bug-fixing cover reading and predicting, while writing is only modeled in the worked example.

The sort activity's prompt says 'This loop adds up the numbers in nums' but never displays the code, and placing the line 'for n in nums:' in the 'Outside the loop (runs once)' bucket is defensible yet ambiguous — the loop header could reasonably be read as part of the loop, which may confuse rather than clarify.

The third check's retry ('Strings accumulate the same way numbers do: start empty, append one piece per trip, print once at the end') restates the same pattern structure as the first check's retry; it is a fair hint but not a distinctly different explanation angle.
